item.title: Indians in NL urge cabinet to speak out on “Cockroach” crackdown
item.description:
Indians in NL urge cabinet to speak out on “Cockroach” crackdown

October 26, 2026 Louis Gore-Langton

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Indians living in the Netherlands are protesting for political solidarity and media attention to the ongoing “Cockroach” protests sweeping India, which are being met with a brutal crackdown by state forces.

The protests erupted in the summer over suspected corruption in the education system and have since turned to focus on changes in the voting system. Young Indians say they are being denied their democratic rights – something protesters say particularly affects minority groups and women.

Indians are a significant part of the Netherlands’ international community, with the statistics office CBS counting about 54,500 Indian nationals in the country – roughly 3.2% of all foreign nationals.

The Progressive Indians Europe group, based in Amsterdam, gathered in The Hague recently to call for recognition of the injustices they say Narendra Modi’s government is inflicting on its people.

A spokesperson for the group told Dutch News that it was asking the Dutch government to publicly stand up for the democratic principles and human rights commitments it recognises in its own foreign policy.

“These developments directly affect people in the Netherlands,” they said. “Our families, friends and communities remain connected to India. What happens there has real consequences for the people we care about, while the precedent set by the erosion of electoral safeguards matters to democracies everywhere.”

The suppression of the Cockroach movement, the group says, which has seen thousands arrested, journalists detained, and reports of widespread police brutality, means people in the Netherlands should “examine the reporting, listen to affected communities and recognise the importance of independent investigations, transparency and accountability.”

The group stressed that it was not asking people to accept every allegation without scrutiny.

“We hope it encourages the Dutch public, media and policymakers to engage seriously with these developments and recognise that defending democracy is a shared international responsibility.”

A spokesperson for the foreign affairs ministry told Dutch News: “The Netherlands follows the developments in India. As human rights and democracy are an important part of the Strategic Partnership between India and the Netherlands, the Netherlands and India discuss these topics regularly in diplomatic contacts and will continue to do so.”

Struck off
Some of the members said the situation abroad is significantly impacting their lives. Surabhi, from Amsterdam, said she takes her right to vote very seriously, both in India and in Dutch municipal elections.

“I am an Indian national and have always travelled back to India to vote,” she said. “Most recently, I voted in the national elections in 2024 and the municipality elections in Mumbai in January 2026.”

Her name, along with millions of others, has been removed during a revision of the electoral rolls by the Election Commission of India, which says it is improving the voting system by removing dead, duplicate and ineligible voters.

Another protester, Anubhav, described how he can only see the voting list on the Election Commission of India website by using a VPN. When he saw his name had been removed, he submitted a complaint, which was closed the very next day.

He says he is a “popular anti-BJP [the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party] guy on social media among my acquaintances. Is this just a coincidence? I don’t know.”

Cockroach movement
The Cockroach Janta Party, whose name plays on that of Modi’s BJP, started in May as an online satire account. It was a response to India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, describing some activists and unemployed young people as “cockroaches” and “parasites of society”. Kant later said his remarks had been misquoted and misrepresented.

In July, Modi’s education minister was forced to resign in the wake of street protests against leaked exam papers. Amnesty International found that police used pellet-firing shotguns, electric shock batons, tear gas and batons against demonstrators. Delhi police said more than 400 people, including officers, were injured.

The latest wave of protests that began on October 2 was a reaction to a nationwide revision of the voter rolls. According to reports, about 14% of the original names on the rolls – more than 133 million – have been removed since the process began last year. Protesters say eligible voters have been wrongly struck off in favour of the BJP.

The Indian electoral commission says voters removed in error can register again, and has said all its actions were lawful.

More than 2,000 protesters, including several opposition MPs, were detained in Delhi over the weekend of October 10 and 11. On October 13, Human Rights Watch said police had beaten protesters, dragged them through the streets, arbitrarily detained them and suspended mobile internet services.

Police have said protesters were uncooperative and that force was sometimes needed. The UN human rights office has called on the authorities to fully respect the right to peaceful assembly.

Dutch ties with India
Indians make up one of the largest groups of highly skilled migrants from outside the EU, according to statistics bureau CBS. Many work in IT, and more than 300 Indian companies now have a presence in the Netherlands.

The Netherlands is India’s third largest export destination worldwide, the largest in Europe, and the fourth largest investor in India. According to the Indian embassy, merchandise trade stood at $27.8 billion in 2024-2025.

In May this year, Modi visited the Netherlands and, at a roundtable with Dutch business leaders, spoke of a “new golden era in India–Europe relations”, following the conclusion of free trade talks with the bloc. The agreement “between the world’s two largest democratic and responsible powers will become a strong foundation for shared prosperity”, he said.

Before Modi arrived, prime minister Rob Jetten told reporters there were concerns in the Netherlands and other EU countries about developments in India. “It is not only about press freedom, but also about the rights of minorities, who are under severe pressure,” he said, according to de Volkskrant, adding that the concerns were “regularly raised” with India.

India’s foreign ministry later dismissed the remarks as showing a “lack of understanding”.

item.title: Protecting Frisian: trainee teacher numbers more than double
item.description:
Protecting Frisian: trainee teacher numbers more than double

October 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of students electing to train as Frisian language teachers has doubled this year, amid a historic drive to strengthen and revive the Netherlands’ only officially recognised second language.

More than 34 students signed up to take a Frisian teacher training course at Leeuwarden’s hbo college NHL Stenden, either as a minor or part-time element of their studies, according to Omroep Fryslân.

The change signals a growing revival trend as Friesland, often ranked the Netherlands’ culturally proudest province, fights to protect its linguistic identity. Only 10 years ago, experts warned the language was on the verge of extinction.

Geert Driessen, of Radboud University in Nijmegen, said in a 2016 study that it was the “eleventh hour” for the province’s mother tongue – especially in urban areas, where Dutch speaking newcomers increasingly mix with locals.

Between 1994 and 2014, he found, Frisian spoken outside family homes had halved. This led to the founding of Taalplan Frysk 2030, a government-backed scheme to protect the language through education and social initiatives.

The plan has received millions of euros in funding, much of which has gone to NHL Stenden. Recent studies show Frisian comprehension is rising, and since this school year all primary and secondary school pupils in Friesland are actively taught the language.

In September, the University of Groningen also launched the first standalone Frisian language degree in 15 years.

item.title: Sugar rush: blood bank acts to stem flow of free iced biscuits
item.description:
Sugar rush: blood bank acts to stem flow of free iced biscuits

October 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch blood bank Sanquin has had to lock away the iced biscuits it hands out to donors after discovering it was haemorrhaging money through the heartwarming gesture.

A volunteer at the donation point in Delft told Omroep West the organisation had taken the drastic step because some visitors were abusing its generosity. “People were going out of here with their bags full,” they said.

Sanquin’s Instagram page promotes the pink-topped biscuits as a “well-earned tradition” to thank blood donors and restore their blood sugar levels.

But according to volunteers, the gesture is costing it around €1,000 a month in Delft alone, forcing it to put the biscuits behind the counter.

Instead there are now laminated menus in the café telling people they can ask for a biscuit after they have given blood.

Not all Sanquin donation points have withdrawn the biscuits. NOS found they were still on display in Utrecht and at a football club in Utrecht.

A spokesman for Sanquin’s head office said it was up to individual branches to decide, but confirmed that at some locations there were problems with “people taking more than we would reasonably expect.”

A volunteer in The Hague said: “We see people taking more than they should, but if they say they’re taking them home, should we be forbidding that?”

item.title: Van der Burg plans to use more AI so government can cut payroll
item.description:
Van der Burg plans to use more AI so government can cut payroll

October 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Deputy home affairs minister Eric van der Burg has set out plans to cut the number of civil servants by 16% by 2035 in a wide-ranging efficiency drive.

Van der Burg said he wanted to take 25,000 government officials off the payroll by standardising IT systems and using other tools to make government more efficient, including AI.

The VVD minister, whose official title is State Secretary for Decisive Government, also plans to reduce the number of advisory bodies and committees, currently 28 and 150 respectively, he wrote in a letter to parliament.

It is the first time Van der Burg has put a number on the civil service cuts, which the cabinet hopes will save €3.5 billion a year by 2035. The announcement confirms earlier reports in the Telegraaf that the cabinet plans to use AI technologies to streamline the apparatus of government.

The minister has not said which departments will have to bear the brunt of the savings, but the police and the defence budgets are expected to be excluded.

However, government agencies that are currently under strain such as the tax office and the employment benefits agency UWV are not likely to be spared.

Simpler regulation

Van der Burg said some of the savings could be made by having fewer regulations and “exceptions to exceptions”. The cabinet has committed to scrapping 500 rules a year under the coalition agreement drawn up by the D66, VVD and CDA parties.

But he admitted that not all the reductions could be compensated by more efficient methods. “Some choices will have to be made regarding what the government should be doing less or not at all,” Van der Burg said.

He also said the government wanted to tighten the rules around the freedom of information law Woo, which citizens and journalists rely on to access public information.

“The requests for information are frequently so broad that it is no longer clear what information we are supposed to provide,” he wrote.

item.title: International parcels drop by 32% after EU imposes surcharge
item.description:
International parcels drop by 32% after EU imposes surcharge

October 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of parcels sent from outside the EU dropped by one-third in the last three months, mainly as a result of tighter EU restrictions, postal service PostNL said in its latest quarterly report.

The company said the 32% drop mainly reflected a drop in packages being sent from Asia after the bloc imposed a €3 surcharge per product on July 1.

It follows a 15% dip in the second quarter of the year and PostNL expects the trend to continue after the import fees are raised by a further €2 from next month.

The impact was partly offset by a 40% increase in parcels within the EU compared to the third quarter last year as Asian websites lost trade to European rivals because of result of the new measures.

But PostNL said that growth was “more than wiped out” by the drop in deliveries from further afield.

Three-day deliveries

The company’s turnover increased in the third quarter by €6 million to €768 million after the government relaxed the rules on deliveries.

Since July PostNL has been required to deliver letters within two days rather than 24 hours and the deadline is due to be stretched to three days next July.

CEO Pim Berendsen said the move to three-day deliveries was an important  “interim step” towards ensuring the postal service could survive in the long term, but also renewed his calls for the government to compensate the company’s losses in recent years.

“Until we have a future-proofed regulatory framework, the uncertainty for thousands of our postal workers, customers and consumers will continue,” he said. “This situation requires a structural solution.”

item.title: Study of revolutionary feminist wins Libris prize for history
item.description:
Study of revolutionary feminist wins Libris prize for history

October 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A biography of a radical feminist thinker who published a series of influential revolutionary tracts while raising a family of three children has won this year’s prestigious Libris history prize.

Dubbelleven (“Double Life”), a study of the life of the Dutch philosopher Geertruida Kapteyn-Muysken by historian Maite Karssenberg, was praised for “exposing the shockingly subordinate role of women in the 19th century”.

The jury also highlighted Karssenberg’s “completely original” approach to her work, using diaries and letters to recreate Kapteyn-Muysken’s life and lead the reader through the writer’s eight-year trawl through the archives.

Born in Hillegom in 1855 and raised in Haarlem, Kapteyn-Muysken spent 20 years in England with her husband and children before moving to Zürich, where she became known in radical intellectual circles.

She campaigned for votes for women, sexual ethics, pacifism and non-religious education in the early 20th century. After her return to the Netherlands in 1908 she held salons at her home in Scheveningen and counted progressive icons such as Clara Wichmann and Aletta Jacobs among her circle of friends.

“After her death she was praised as ‘one of the most free and unrestrained minds’ of the Dutch revolutionary movement, with an ‘almost universal knowledge of the intellectual and social movements of our time’,” Karssenberg wrote on her website.

Other nominees included Isabel Casteels for De kronieken van de dood; a study of torture and executions in the 16th century; Maarten van Ginderachter for Arm Vlaanderen, which focuses on poverty and famine in 19th-century Flanders; and Dik Verkuil for his biography of the former VVD party leader Frits Bolkestein.

The €20,000 prize is part of the Month of History, organised in collaboration with the magazine Historisch Nieuwsblad and the Dutch Open Air Museum (Nederlands Openluchtmuseum) in Arnhem.

item.title: Leopard attack leaves Beekse Bergen zookeeper critically injured
item.description:
Leopard attack leaves Beekse Bergen zookeeper critically injured

October 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A zookeeper was mauled by a leopard at Beekse Bergen safari park on Saturday, leaving her in critical condition. Medics say she is not expected to survive.

Two Persian panthers, which had been sheltering from the weather, attacked the woman in an enclosure, according to reports. There is no CCTV footage and investigations into what happened are ongoing.

The victim was highly experienced, according to Omroep Brabant, having spent around 25 years working at the park and caring for the animals. She sustained serious wounds to her head and neck from the attack, and her conditioned worsened over Sunday night.

She managed to call for help via a walkie-talkie and was rescued by colleagues before being almost immediately operated on. A trauma helicopter and large numbers of emergency workers rushed to the sight.

It is unclear why or how she was in the enclosure with the animals – something that is never normally allowed.

Wineke Schoo, director of the Dutch Association of Zoos, described the incident as a “worst case scenario” to Omroep Brabant, and said she has only ever experienced one such incident in 25 years of Dutch zookeeping, which was a lion attack in 2001.

item.title: One dead and one missing after Storm Boelo hits NL
item.description:
One dead and one missing after Storm Boelo hits NL

October 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

One person has died and one is missing after Storm Boelo rolled across the Netherlands over the weekend from the North Sea. The storm forced mass flight cancellations at Schiphol and wreaked havoc across the coastlines.

The KNMI issued a code yellow weather warning for high winds, which reached gale force 9 on Sunday, rising up to 115km per hour in some places, such as IJmuiden. It marks the year’s first official named storm.

One man was killed by a falling tree in Amsterdam Nieuw-West, and a water sports player went missing off the coast of Scheveningen. Rescue efforts were suspended due to the weather and resumed on Monday morning.

On the island of Texel, Oudeschild harbour flooded on Sunday evening as the seawater broke over the quays. Wind gusts were recorded at up to 90km per hour around the Wadden Islands.

Rain caused local flooding in The Hague and Voorhout, while fallen trees caused disruption in Katwijk, Delft, ‘s-Gravenzande and Rijswijk.

A number of roads throughout the country were also closed off to protect traffic from debris. The N207 near Alphen aan den Rijn was closed in both directions after multiple trees came down, and the N33 between Appingedam and Siddeburen in Groningen was closed in both directions as a precaution.

Two people in the UK were also killed by storm Boelo by falling trees, one in London and one in Scotland. Widespread damage was also recorded throughout Britain.

item.title: Bosz frustrated as Feyenoord hold PSV to 1-1 draw in Eindhoven
item.description:
Bosz frustrated as Feyenoord hold PSV to 1-1 draw in Eindhoven

October 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Feyenoord preserved their four-point advantage over champions PSV after coming away with a point from Eindhoven thanks to an improved second-half performance.

PSV dominated the first half as they deployed a close-passing, tiki-taka style to stifle Feyenoord, but only had Guus Til’s well-taken volley after 20 minutes to show for it.

Ten minutes after the break Feyenoord equalised when Anis Hadj Moussa was given too much space to charge down the right flank and bend a shot inside the far post.

The Algerian had a good chance for a second towards the end, while PSV goalkeeper Matej Kovar had to be alert to keep out a header by Nacho Ferri from close range.

“We were by far the better team today and had the better chances,” said PSV coach Peter Bosz. “We started the second half badly and made a mistake, after which Hadj Moussa scored. And even then we could have won it.”

Ajax go second

Ajax overtook PSV to close the gap at the top to three points with a hard-fought win at Sparta. Veteran striker Jens Toornstra scored for Sparta on his 500th Eredivisie appearance, but Abdellah Ouazane and Tolu Arokodare, the scorers against Atalanta in midweek, were on target again to claim the win for Ajax.

Twente moved up to fourth place as two late goals by Sondre Ørjasæter and Lucas Vennegoor of Hesselink earned a 2-0 win at AZ Alkmaar, who like Twente and PSV have 20 points.

Fortuna Sittard also snatched the points late on against Excelsior as Rodrigo Guth headed in a corner in injury time to keep the Limburg club in sixth place, two points further back.

At the other end of the table, the return of Adrie Koster as veteran coach brought no relief to Willem II, who crashed to a 6-1 home defeat to Cambuur.

The Tilburgers remain four points behind ADO Den Haag, who were unable to keep up the momentum of last week’s win against PSV as they lost 3-2 at home to Heerenveen.

Telstar lost by the same margin at Go Ahead Eagles, whose striker Søren Tengstedt netted twice in the first half to lead the Eredivisie scoring charts with eight goals.

item.title: More sleep on Sunday as clocks go back an hour
item.description:
More sleep on Sunday as clocks go back an hour

October 24, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Everyone is due an extra hour’s sleep on Sunday as the clocks will roll back an hour at 3am to 2am.

Daylight saving time in the Netherlands has been in place since 1977, following the oil crisis of the 70s, when saving energy on lighting became a priority.

The clocks go forward in spring, on the last Sunday of March, to give lighter evenings. Staying on summer time into the winter would mean very dark mornings, so in October the clocks return to standard time.

The EU has debated ending daylight saving time altogether and the European Parliament voted to stop it in 1996 but member states have not yet committed to it.

So tomorrow you can lie in a little longer.
